Course Home/Optimize existing feature strategy

24 mins ● 3 steps

Optimize existing feature strategy

Fareed Mosavat

Product & Growth Advisor, Podcast Host & Course Lead at Reforge

Casey Winters

Advisor at Whatnot and Faire, Partner at Reforge

Overview

It’s common for many product leaders to focus on product-level analysis. While this is important to understanding the overall performance of a product, it often lacks feature-specific insights. Bad features can be hidden by strong product performance and good features can be hidden by overall poor product performance.

Features take up product surface area and user mindshare. So they need to earn their keep by both being individually viable and accretive to the overall experience. When evaluating features, product leaders should constantly evaluate "How does this feature contribute to the overall success of the product and company?”

By optimizing your feature bundle, you can maximize the value your product delivers to users. This is crucial for achieving feature product fit and fulfilling your product's core use case.

What you'll do

  • Qualitatively define features.
  • Quantitatively measure feature performance (adoption, retention, user satisfaction).
  • Assess overall feature bundle.

Get strategic advice backed by Reforge's knowledge base, personalized to you.

Beta

Start a conversation with suggested prompts, tailored to you:

1

Qualitatively define features

Qualitatively defining features is important because it informs how we later measure feature performance, as well as how we interpret the results.

Not defining your feature qualitatively leads to making the wrong strategic decisions. If we put garbage in, we're just going to get garbage out.

To qualitatively evaluate features, we recommend creating a feature map for each feature in your bundle. You can also ask PMs on your team to draft the first version for their features and then align on a final version together.

There are three areas of a feature map that are important to define: the target population, user value, and business value.

Identify the target

There are two things we want to define with the target population: target description and target size.

  • Target description: A qualitative description of what target segment your feature is designed for. We can define a target segment based on a variety of factors, and we need to be able to identify these factors in our data.

    Some examples include product use cases, user demographics, level of product engagement, level of product experience, and customer type.
  • Target size: The estimated percentage of our active user base on the whole product that our target segment represents. This puts a quantitative value on the size of the identified target segment, giving you a clearer picture of the potential impact of your feature and helping you to prioritize development efforts.

    To do this, we should only count target users who are active users of the product.

    If we don't filter for active users of the product, we won't get a good sense of whether issues are due to the specific feature or something at the product level.

Determine user value

The next category on our feature map is user value. This describes how the feature adds value for the user. The three key components to consider in this step are the user problem description, the frequency of the user problem, and the severity of the user problem.

  • User problem description: Start by identifying what user problem your feature addresses. This step requires a clear understanding of your end-user needs and challenges. The user problem description should be succinct and focused, highlighting the core issue that the feature aims to resolve.
  • Frequency of the user problem: It’s important to note that features don't always have the same natural frequency as our overall product. In order to evaluate feature retention, we need to know how often that individual feature should be used. To form a qualitative hypothesis on the natural frequency we would ask users questions like: What problem does the feature solve for you? When was the last time you experienced that problem? The time before that? And the time before that?

    After getting them to recall a few times they experienced the problem, we can have them estimate how frequently they think they encounter the problem in their life.
  • The severity of the user problem: We can assess problem severity by asking a few different questions to arrive at a t-shirt sizing (low/medium/high).

Evaluate business value

Considering business value requires us to define two components: business impact and strategic importance.

  • Business impact: To evaluate the business impact of your feature, you need to identify whether the feature is defensively or offensively oriented.

    Offensive features are those that proactively drive a product KPI, specifically acquisition, retention, or monetization. They add value to the product at a net level, meaning after any cannibalization effects, these features improve KPIs. Both Eventbrite's embedded checkout and Slack's shared channel are examples of offensive-focused features.

    Defensive features are those that are required for the product to function properly or meet minimum market requirements (MMRs). The cancel feature in Uber could be viewed as one required to make the product function properly. Notion syncing across devices is a feature that meets MMRs. These features may not directly improve key performance indicators (KPIs), but they prevent them from decreasing.
  • Strategic importance: This can be assessed based on how closely it aligns with your company's long-term goals and its potential to unlock future opportunities. Features that are considered to be of higher strategic importance include those that are designed for larger target segments, address more severe problems, and directly contribute to a product’s value proposition.

Example

|

Low vs high severity

Examples of low severity:

  • Splitwise is an app that lets users track and split expenses with friends. It does not support native payments. Providing native payments as a feature in the app may be considered low severity, as Splitwise provides a simple workaround to users by easily linking out to PayPal and Venmo.
  • Spotify's web app does not allow web users to save podcasts to their playlists. Users instead could use their mobile app or could listen to the podcast directly using the web app. Since there is a workaround, saving podcasts on the web app may be considered low severity.

Examples of high severity:

  • Swiping on Tinder is critical to users gaining value from the overall product as it directly leads to matches. Any problem related to the swiping experience would therefore be considered high severity.
  • So is DocuSign's electronic signature feature, which allows users to asynchronously sign documents. The signing feature is core to the creation and capture of value for users of this product. Any problems related to this experience would therefore be considered high severity.

Example

|

Eventbrite qualitative feature map

Let’s consider Eventbrite's embedded checkout, which allows event creators to build an inline checkout into their websites.

Here’s how an Eventbrite product leader might go about defining the feature map for this feature:

Target Population

  • Target Description: Event creators with paid accounts that create new events and have a website where they intend to sell tickets.
  • Target Size: Hypothetically, let's estimate Eventbrite's embedded checkout target size is 10% of active users.

User Value

  • User Problem Description: Creators want to sell event tickets directly on their professional websites. Creators could want their audience to have the purchasing experience through their own website and branding so that they own that end-to-end relationship.
  • User Problem Frequency: Interestingly, this is a set-and-forget feature. Once customers embed Eventbrite's checkout into their website, the feature is up and running and does not require further modification -- the functionality remains embedded on their site. To think about frequency, we want to monitor that it stays embedded on their website.
  • User Problem Severity: Moderate to high user problem severity as the feature solves an important problem for its target segment of users. Without it, a segment of users cannot experience the core value prop of the Eventbrite product. While there is an alternative workaround, the Eventbrite API, it requires a lot more effort to use.

Business Value

  • Business Impact: Embedded checkout drives acquisition and some creators sign up for Eventbrite for this specific feature. It also drives retention, as the target segment would likely leave for other platforms if it didn't exist. And finally, it drives monetization, as it's included in one of the premium tiers and drives upgrades.
  • Strategic Importance: Moderate to high. As the business impact is high, the target segment of users is an important one for Eventbrite and they would likely not use the product without the feature.

Example

|

Slack qualitative feature map

The second example we'll look at is Slack's shared channel feature, which allows users to communicate with people from external companies or organizations.

Here’s how a Slack product leader might go about defining the feature map for this feature:

Target Population

  • Target Description: Engaged Slack users who have frequent high-priority communication with people outside of the company.
  • Target Size: Let's assume that it's 20%.

User Value

  • User Problem Description: Shared channels are aimed at solving the problem of communicating with external stakeholders with Slack. This could be any specific user problem involving collaboration across customer success, business development deals, sales implementations, vendor relationships, or other types of use cases.
  • User Problem Frequency: Target users will likely face a need to communicate externally on a weekly basis. Therefore, the feature problem frequency is weekly.
  • User Problem Severity: Many users view the problem that shared channels resolve as important to their use of Slack. As an alternative, users could use email, but Slack allows for a much faster, more casual way to collaborate.

Business Value

  • Business Impact: Slack's shared channel feature helps acquire new users, as one company invites others from another company, and then that company might start to adopt Slack for its own internal use. In addition, the feature is included in Slack's premium tier, helping drive conversions to paying subscribers.
  • Strategic Importance: High strategic importance because it paved the way for Slack Connect. While shared channels allowed collaboration with external stakeholders, it was not easy to use when there were more than two companies. So Slack addressed this issue by creating Slack Connect to enable multi-party collaboration use cases.

Tip

|

Start narrow with target population scope

When looking at all of these different ways to define the segment, a common question that comes up is: “how narrowly or wide should I scope this target population?”. This comes up because oftentimes many users end up using a feature even if it's not specifically designed for them.

We can break users into three key categories:

  • Core users: these are the users whom your feature is specifically designed to create value for. Most users who discover and get into an initial habit with your product will stay in that habit because there is a clear value for them.
  • Adjacent users: these are the users who may find value in your product, but for whatever reason have not become regular users. These users are within reach with some nurturing.
  • Non-adjacent users: these are non-users of the feature. They do not use the feature and the feature was not really designed to solve the problem that they're facing.

One challenge here is that a target segment is not always binary. There is often a primary target segment of core users who get the most value from a feature, and then adjacent users that get some value out of the feature.

How you define your target segment has big implications on what your adoption metric is and how you evaluate it.

If you start by evaluating how effective your feature is for a target segment that includes adjacent or non adjacent users, you might see poor adoption retention or satisfaction metrics driven by your adjacent or non-adjacent users while you're trying to understand how effective your feature is for core users.

On the flip side, if your feature adoption, retention, and satisfaction look great for your core users, you want to start evaluating how you broaden that audience to ensure that your feature is valuable for as many users as possible.

So a good rule of thumb is to start with your most primary target segment, the core users that you design this feature for. Define your target segment as the group of users who are most likely to get value from your feature.

Once adoption, retention, and satisfaction are very high for your target segment, you can start to expand your measurement and evaluate the performance of your feature relative to larger adjacent segments.

2

Quantitatively measure feature performance

After qualitatively evaluating your features, you can more easily measure performance.

We can model feature effectiveness with a framework called TARS. TARS stands for:

  • the Target population for a feature
  • the share of the target users who Adopt a feature
  • the share of adopted users who are Retained
  • and the share of retained users who are Satisfied.

In this guide, we’ll focus on how to measure each component of TARS.

🔗 Optional: For more in-depth guidance on evaluating and improving each component, check out the “Evaluate Feature Performance” guide.

Target population

The first metric to define in the TARS framework is your target population.

Luckily, you can leverage the existing thinking in your feature map, specifically the Target Size field.

Feature adoption

Once you've defined your target population, the next step is to measure feature adoption. Adoption is a proxy for how effectively your feature is surfaced and communicated to the target population of active users.

This involves:

  • Defining adoption event: This answers the question: “When is a user considered to adopt a feature?”
  • Calculating adoption percentage: Take the ratio of active adopted users to active target users.

Feature retention

After measuring adoption, the next step is to measure feature retention. Feature retention is an indicator of how well your feature solves the problem for the user. This involves:

  • Determining natural frequency: Identify how often users experience the problem the feature solves. Luckily, you would have already formed a qualitative hypothesis when building the feature map.
  • Defining the core action: This is the action that demonstrates users are getting value from your product.
  • Building a retention curve chart: Plot the percentage of adopted users active at each natural frequency interval. For example, if a feature's natural frequency is monthly, we can see how many users are still using the feature one, two, or three months later.
  • Visualizing the chart: We can set up a chart where the Y axis is the percentage of adopted users that are still active, and the X axis is time-based on the natural frequency intervals. Look for when the retention curve stabilizes. If the retention curve never stabilizes, that is a clear case of a retention problem.

Feature satisfaction

While retention is a good indicator of whether the feature is solving the problem it was designed for, there are instances where features are used, but the experience of using them is still extremely frustrating. This is why we measure feature satisfaction.

Common approaches like NPS and the Sean Ellis test, which asks “How would you feel if our product no longer contained this feature?”, often fall short. For example, NPS tends to work better for products than features.

Hence we recommend the Customer Effort Score (CES), commonly used to measure customer effort required to experience a service or use of a product.

Example

|

Eventbrite TARS

Let’s again consider Eventbrite's embedded checkout, which allows event creators to build an inline checkout into their websites.

  • Target Population: Based on the feature map, the target description could be event creators with paid accounts that create new events and have a website where they intend to sell tickets, and the target size could be 10% of active users.
  • Adoption: The adoption event could be when an event creator has added the embedded checkout to their website.
  • Retention:
    • From the feature map, the natural frequency is weekly.
    • Since this is a set-and-forget feature, the core action might be defined as creators continuing to have the embedded checkout functionality on their websites.
  • Satisfaction: This may be gauged by asking creators, “Overall, how easy was it for you to sell tickets directly on your website using the embedded checkout feature today?”

Example

|

Slack TARS

The second example we'll look at is Slack's shared channel feature, which allows users to communicate with people from external companies or organizations.

  • Target Population: From the feature map, we can conclude that these are Slack users with external team members, which is ~15% of all active users.
  • Adoption: For a user to message in a shared channel for the first time, meaning they've gone through the setup of a shared channel, including inviting others and exchanging that first message.
  • Retention:
    • We can see the user problem frequency for Slack Shared Channel by looking at the feature map we filled out. In this case, it was weekly.
    • The core action is similar to the adoption event, which is sending a message in the shared time.
  • Satisfaction: Users might get asked, “Overall, how easy was it for you to collaborate with external team members using shared channels today?”

Tip

|

TARS best practices

  • Target Population: Only count target users who are active users of the product. If we don't filter for active users of the product, we won't get a good sense of whether issues with adoption, retention, or satisfaction of the feature are due to the specific feature or something at the product level.
  • Feature Adoption: In many cases, having high adoption is a positive indicator of your feature. However, there is one primary situation where you may need to investigate further: when you have too narrowly defined your target population. Here, the solution is to more broadly define that target segment.
  • Feature Retention: Feature nature frequency may differ from product natural frequency. Especially as you build more features, their problem frequency becomes less likely to be as prominent as the overall product frequency. So you end up with a bunch of these features that people don't need to use as often as they use the entire product.
  • Feature Satisfaction: Even if you only focus on retained users, it’s unlikely you will be able to collect this data from all users. So you will have to use the users' responses from a sample population to estimate your overall population satisfaction.

3

Assess the overall feature bundle

Everything so far in our TARS framework has been about evaluating features on an individual basis and identifying individual strategies.

But it's helpful to get a bird's eye view of all the features within a product and view those features as a bundle.

So the final step is to assess your overall feature bundle. This involves viewing your features collectively on a feature matrix and determining how they contribute to your product's value proposition.

Calculate the S/T score

The Satisfaction-to-Target (S/T) score measures what percentage of your target user audience is satisfied with the feature. To calculate the S/T score, you divide the percentage of satisfied users by the percentage of target users for each feature.

For example, if we had a TARS evaluation that had a:

  • Target audience of 80%,
  • and then 50% of the target audience adopted, or 40% of the total,
  • and then 70% of adopted users retained, which is 28% of the total,
  • and then 90% of retained users are satisfied.

The S/T score for the feature would be 25% divided by 80%, which is 31%.

Plot the matrix

We can then plot the S/T score vs strategic importance on a 2x2 matrix, where the S/T score is on the Y-axis and strategic importance is on X-axis.

For strategic importance, it's common to default to scoring things as "Medium", which can lead to many medium-importance features being hard to differentiate. To prevent this, take your initial scores and stack rank them relative to other features. This way, you have them listed from highest strategic importance to lowest.

Use the feature matrix

We can loosely categorize this graph into four quadrants and form a feature matrix.

The upper right-hand corner is your core features. The lower right corner is your liability features. The upper left corner is your over-performing features. The bottom left-hand corner is your project features.

  • Core Features: Generally, you want to see your highest strategic importance features concentrated in the top right “Core Features” quadrant, showing that these are also your highest satisfaction ones. A good next step here would be to maximize value capture or expand the target audience to try to replicate the feature's success with a broader group.
  • Liability Features: What you want to avoid most is having strategically important features in the “Liability Features” quadrant, indicating low satisfaction. These features should be prioritized as they require a lot of iteration and feedback to move up the gap in key feature metrics
  • Project Features: While these aren't as dire to fix given their lower strategic importance, they are also an area where product leaders can provide the most clarity to their team on which should be invested in and which should be considered to be killed or replaced.
  • Overperforming Features: Like core features, product leaders should push overperforming features to either maximize value capture or expand the target audience.

Leverage core features

You can create more value with core features specifically by either driving more monetization or strengthening the acquisition or retention of the overall product.

  • Driving more monetization: An example of this is Twitch Bits. Twitch Bits allows viewers to donate to streamers. It was a very highly adopted, retained, and satisfied feature, and as a result, Twitch monetized it by taking a cut.
  • Strengthen acquisition or retention: Snapchat lenses are an example of a feature that strengthens both acquisition through virality and retention through higher engagement. Also, Venmo's payment feed likely facilitated a social environment for sharing in peer-to-peer payments strengthening Venmo's virality.

Example

|

Slack S/T score

Let's hypothetically run the same analysis for Slack's shared channels.

We previously made the assumption that the target population was 20% of Slack's active users.

Given that the feature has high problem severity for its target audience, let's assume that 90% of the target population adopts the feature and 85% of those adopted are retained.

This means that 18% (20% * 90%) of the product's active users have adopted shared channels and 15% (20% * 90%* 85%) have retained.

Finally, we'll assume that 98% of those retained have high satisfaction, meaning that 15% (20% * 90% * 85% * 98%) of active users have high satisfaction.

The S/T score would therefore in this case be 15% divided by 20%, which equals 75%.

Given that the high S/T score of 75% and the previously defined high strategic importance, we can place the shared channels feature in the Core Features quadrant.

Example

|

Eventbrite S/T score

Returning to the Eventbrite embedded checkout feature, let’s assume 70% of the target population adopted the feature, and out of those, 50% retained it (meaning they kept the feature active on their site), and 90% report being satisfied.

In defining the qualitative feature map, we previously sized the target population as 10% of active users. We also ranked the strategic importance as moderate to high, considering its unique value proposition and its role in Eventbrite's premium offerings.

This means that 7% (10% * 70%) of the product's active users have adopted embedded checkout and 3.5% (10% * 70% * 50%) have retained it.

We can then calculate that 3% (10% * 70% * 50% * 90%) of active users have high satisfaction.

Therefore, the S/T score is 3% divided by 10%, or 30%.

This would make the embedded checkout a potential liability feature. To improve this feature, the Eventbrite product team will need to iterate and improve the feature performance, starting with looking at why retention is only 50%.

Tip

|

Niche features

Expanding the target audience is especially relevant for niche features.

Niche features are features that have good adopted, retained, and satisfied scores, but target a low percentage of the overall active user base. Therefore, these are features that are designed for a very small group of users, but that small group really likes it and has high satisfaction.

Therefore, in order to keep a niche feature, you need to make sure that it:

  • is designed for a target user population that is strategically valuable to the company.
  • adds significant value to the product as a whole, not just the target user population.
  • is not unnecessarily difficult or costly to maintain.

An example of this is Slack's interactive screen-sharing feature, which allows multiple users in video screen share to be able to move their cursor around. This feature gained a devout following a niche target audience, specifically remote companies with a pair-programming ethos.

But this was a specific segment of power users. While these users liked the feature, their level of engagement was unlikely to change with or without the feature in the overall product. Given the complexity of maintaining this feature, Slack eventually discontinued it.

Recap

  • Qualitatively define features. Consider the target population, user value, and business value of each feature in your bundle. Doing this step first will make it easier to determine how to quantitatively measure feature performance next.
  • Quantify feature performance using the TARS framework. Define the target population, measure feature adoption and retention, and assess feature satisfaction to comprehensively understand each feature's performance.
  • Assess your overall feature bundle using a feature matrix. Calculate the Satisfaction-to-Target (S/T) score for each feature and plot them on a matrix against strategic importance. Use this matrix to identify core, liability, overperforming, and project features.
